excerpt: Meridian is an on-device AI work journal for developers: it reconstructs your day from screen activity, matches it to Jira and GitHub tickets and drafts standups and worklog updates for you to approve. Source-available since a licence change in October 2026. How it works, privacy and alternatives.
content:
Meridian is a desktop work journal for developers. It runs in the background, builds a timeline of your day from on-screen activity, matches the work to open Jira and GitHub tickets, and drafts a worklog update, a standup note and a daily summary. Nothing is posted until you approve it. The makers' point is that developers do a lot of unplanned work that never reaches a ticket, so an AI asked to write an update misses it; Meridian records it as it happens, including terminal work over SSH, and lets you look back at any past day.

According to its README, activity is kept in an encrypted database on your machine, analysis runs through the AI provider you connect, and only what a summary needs is sent to it. You can bring the Claude Code, Cursor or Codex CLI you already use, or Groq for free. It needs screen recording and accessibility permissions, runs on macOS (Apple silicon) and Windows 10/11, and the README lists 0.5 to 3 GB of memory and about 20 GB of storage a month, pruned after 30 days. Meridian launched as MIT-licensed open source. On 6 October 2026 its GitHub repository was relicensed to the PolyForm Strict License 1.0.0, which is source-available rather than open source: the README says you may read the code and use it for personal and other noncommercial purposes, may not modify or redistribute it, and need a separate licence from Meridiona for commercial use, including use inside a company. Versions released before the change remain under MIT. The website, which still has an 'Open source' link in its footer, now presents Meridian as an engineering-intelligence workspace for teams.

Meridian is made by Meridiona LLP, founded by Akarsh Hegde and Adithya Harish. It launched on Product Hunt on 17 August 2026 and finished #1 for the day with 536 upvotes and 99 comments.

We have not tested Meridian ourselves. This page brings together Meridian's website, GitHub README and licence, its Product Hunt page and launch discussion, and says where each fact comes from.

profile.starts_at: Free for personal, noncommercial use; commercial licence not priced
profile.summary_short: On-device work journal that drafts standups and Jira updates from your day's activity

gallery.alt: Meridian timeline of a developer's day with tasks matched to tickets, captioned 'You did more than you think'
Meridian graphic contrasting three planned tasks on the ticket with three planned plus four unplanned in the actual day
Meridian daily summary with completed tasks, unexpected work and a standup ready to paste
Meridian drafting a worklog for a Jira ticket that is posted only after you approve it

paragraphs: Akarsh Hegde says he quit his job three months before launch to build Meridian. He and his co-founder kept asking Claude to write updates and then spending ten minutes adding back the context it had missed: the unexpected problems they had solved along the way. A Reddit post he wrote about developers underestimating unplanned work went viral.

Meridian does the remembering: it groups the day into a timeline, matches work to Jira and GitHub tickets and drafts the update. He stressed that nothing leaves the device until you approve, that it is free for individual developers, and that it runs on the AI coding CLI you already have.
launch_story.attribution: Akarsh Hegde, founder, on Product Hunt

use_cases: Getting a standup note written from what you actually did yesterday
Drafting Jira worklog updates, including unplanned work, for one-click approval
Finding where the time went when a task took longer than estimated
Looking back at what you worked on on a past day

fit: are a developer who works across Jira, GitHub and the terminal
already use Claude Code, Cursor or Codex CLI, or are happy to use Groq
want a record of unplanned work to show in reviews
not_fit: use an Intel Mac: the README says only Apple silicon is supported
are not comfortable granting screen recording and accessibility permissions
want to use or modify it at work without a commercial licence: the PolyForm Strict License allows only noncommercial use and no changes

pricing.intro: At launch the makers said Meridian was free for individual developers. Since the October 2026 licence change, the README allows only personal and other noncommercial use without a separate licence; commercial use, including use inside a company, needs a licence from Meridiona, and the website offers demos for teams without published prices.

plans.name: Personal (noncommercial)
plans.detail: Desktop app for macOS and Windows; uses your own AI CLI or Groq

notes: Team and commercial pricing is not published; the site offers demo calls.
Versions released before 6 October 2026 remain available under the MIT License, according to the README.

alternatives.intro: Product Hunt lists Rize, Pieces for Developers and Littlebird among Meridian's alternatives. Review scores are Product Hunt users' own; check each tool's pricing page for current prices.

items.name: Rize
items.difference: Tracks time and focus; Meridian writes the work up and drafts ticket updates.

items.name: Pieces for Developers
items.what: On-device AI assistant with long-term memory of your workflow
items.difference: Broader developer memory and snippets; Meridian focuses on standups and Jira or GitHub updates.

items.name: Littlebird
items.what: AI assistant that already knows your work
items.difference: A general assistant with work context; Meridian is built around ticket updates for developers.

alternatives.more: Product Hunt also lists Magicflow and Shadow.

liked: Productivity tracking that is not surveillance-based
A clear picture of how the day was spent
asked: Why an account is needed and why it needs screen and accessibility access (the account counts users; activity stays on device)
Whether it works over SSH on a remote VM (yes, through terminal activity)
How much memory it uses (built in Rust; the README lists 0.5 to 3 GB)
criticised: AI timeouts while drafting (the team said this was fixed)
Required permissions sit uneasily with a privacy-first claim, one commenter said

quotes.text: I haven't seen another product that focuses on individual productivity tracking without being surveillance-based.
quotes.author: Rohan Chaubey

quotes.text: end of busy day? did you get done what needed doing?
quotes.author: Andy Da Costa

pros: Captures unplanned work that never reaches a ticket
Nothing is posted until you approve it
Uses the AI CLI you already pay for, or free Groq
cons: Needs screen recording and accessibility permissions
Uses about 20 GB of storage a month before pruning
Relicensed on 6 October 2026 from MIT to the source-available PolyForm Strict License; use inside a company needs a separate licence

quotes.author: ingrid.e
quotes.text: Questioned why an account and broad permissions are needed for a privacy-first app.
quotes.reply: Adithya Harish said the account only counts usage, screen and accessibility access build the timeline, audio is not recorded, and nothing is stored on their servers.

x.none: We found no posts about Meridian on X to link yet.

faq.a: A desktop work journal for developers that reconstructs your day from screen activity, matches it to Jira and GitHub tickets and drafts standups and worklog updates for you to approve.

For personal and other noncommercial use, yes. Since the October 2026 licence change, the README says commercial use, including use inside a company, needs a separate licence from Meridiona; team pricing is not published.

faq.q: Does my data leave my computer?
faq.a: Activity is stored in an encrypted local database. Summaries are generated by the AI provider you connect, which receives only what a summary needs.
macOS on Apple silicon and Windows 10/11. Intel Macs are not supported.

Not any more. It launched under the MIT License, but on 6 October 2026 the GitHub repository was relicensed to the PolyForm Strict License 1.0.0, a source-available licence that bars changes, redistribution and commercial use. Earlier versions remain under MIT.
Product Hunt lists Rize, Pieces for Developers, Magicflow, Littlebird and Shadow.
